topic.subject: science
topic.title: Work and energy
topic.scope: work in physics, kinetic and potential energy, conservation of energy, power, commercial unit of energy

misconceptions.statement: If a person is tired after pushing a wall, they have done a lot of work.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the biological effort and fatigue with the scientific definition of work.
misconceptions.fix: In physics, work is only done when a force causes an object to move in the direction of the force.

probe.question: A student pushes a heavy cupboard for 10 minutes but it does not move. How much work is done?
probe.wrong_answer: A large amount of work because the student is sweating and tired.

misconceptions.statement: Work is done whenever a force is applied to an object.
misconceptions.why: Students often ignore the requirement of displacement in the formula W = Fs cos(theta).
misconceptions.fix: Work is only done if the object actually changes its position due to the applied force.

probe.question: A man holds a heavy suitcase stationary in his hand. Is he doing work?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because he is applying an upward force to hold the suitcase.

misconceptions.statement: Objects at rest have no energy.
misconceptions.why: Students equate energy only with motion, ignoring stored potential energy.
misconceptions.fix: Energy can be stored in an object due to its position or configuration, which is called potential energy.

probe.question: Does a stone kept on the roof of a building have energy?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is not moving.

misconceptions.statement: Energy is used up or lost when an object stops moving.
misconceptions.why: Students observe objects slowing down and assume the energy simply disappears.
misconceptions.fix: Energy is never lost; it is transformed into other forms like heat or sound due to friction.

probe.question: A ball rolling on the ground eventually stops. Where did its kinetic energy go?
probe.wrong_answer: It is used up and gone forever.

misconceptions.statement: Power and energy are the same thing.
misconceptions.why: In daily life, the terms are used interchangeably to describe how 'strong' or 'active' something is.
misconceptions.fix: Energy is the capacity to do work, while power is the rate at which that work is done.

probe.question: If two motors do the same amount of work, do they have the same power?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they did the same amount of work.
